intro: Stuttgart's old trees are scattered across the whole city rather than clustered in one district, from a churchyard lime in Rohracker to a 6.72-metre ash at Schloss Solitude, a duke's 1779 plane at Hohenheim and an oak in Zuffenhausen that was already called stately in 1711. The one tight pairing is on the Bopser slope, where an oak planted in 1865 on the Schillerhöhe lookout stands about 250 metres from two giant sequoias. Every tree here is free to see, most from open parks, churchyards and squares, one pair only from the street.
meta_description: Stuttgart's ancient trees: an oak named in 1711, a 6.72m ash at Schloss Solitude, Schiller's oak, giant sequoias, a duke's plane and more. All free.
question_meta: Stuttgart's oldest tree by its record is likely the Jahneiche, a Zuffenhausen oak said to be stately already in 1711. Where it stands and how sure that is.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Stuttgart by its written record is likely the Jahneiche, a pedunculate oak in Zuffenhausen that the German Wikipedia says was already a stately old tree in 1711, which puts it at over 300 years. That date rests on one account, so the best measured figure belongs to the Ash at Schloss Solitude, put at roughly 250 years from its 6.72-metre girth.
question_context: The Jahneiche's age rests on one account: the German Wikipedia says Duke Eberhard Ludwig of Württemberg built a hunting pavilion beside it in 1711, when it was already a stately old tree. We have not seen the record behind that, so this page carries the age as over 300 years with no upper figure; nobody has measured the trunk. The Solitude ash is the best measured: the register baumkunde.de put its trunk at 6.72 metres round in May 2026 and estimated 250 years from that girth, which this page carries as a band of 200 to 300 years. The Hohenheim Love Plane was planted in 1779 and the Schillereiche in 1865. The Hutteneiche carries a story to 1515, but no source claims the standing tree is the oak of that legend, so no age follows from it. The Oberdorfplatz Mulberry, the Kurpark's bald cypresses and the Wernhalde sequoias are documented only by their 2003 designation, which records when the city started protecting them, not when they were planted. Where an age is unknown, this page says so and asks anyone who knows to tell us.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Stuttgart?
faq.a: Probably the Jahneiche in Zuffenhausen, an oak the German Wikipedia describes as already stately in 1711, so over 300 years old; that rests on one account. The best measured is the Ash at Schloss Solitude, put at roughly 250 years from its 6.72-metre girth.

faq.q: Are Stuttgart's ancient trees clustered together?
faq.a: Mostly not. They are spread from Rohracker in the east to Solitude in the west, so treat most as short outings of their own. The exception is the Bopser slope, where the Schillereiche and the Wernhalde sequoias stand about 250 metres apart.

Yes, no ticket is needed for any of them. Most stand on open ground: churchyards, parks, squares, forest and the grounds of Schloss Solitude. The two Wernhalde sequoias stand between houses and are seen from the street.

faq.q: What is the story behind the Hutteneiche?
faq.a: Local tradition says Duke Ulrich of Württemberg hanged his stable master, Hans von Hutten, from an oak here in 1515. No source claims the standing tree is that same individual; the story belongs to the place.

trees.name: The Bernhardskirche Linden
trees.story:
The church was already three centuries old before anyone planted the tree in front of it. Rohracker's Bernhardskirche was built after 1447. The parish's own history says the lime in its garden went in around 1870, which makes it about 150 years old and comfortably the younger of the pair.

Stuttgart designated it a natural monument in 2003 and gave two reasons: its character, and the animals living in it. The register is a little confused about the tree and carries it twice, under two numbers at identical coordinates. The city's own ordinance settles it by naming exactly one lime at Rohrackerstraße 257, so this is one tree with two entries rather than two trees.

What it has witnessed is not a battle or a duke, and that is rather the point. It has stood through the whole of modern Germany in a working village churchyard on Stuttgart's eastern slopes, doing the job churchyard trees have always had: making a patch of shade people sit in. The parish still describes its garden exactly that way, as somewhere to linger, with this lime as the reason it works.

Come in the last week of June or the first of July. Small-leaved limes flower then, the scent carries across the whole garden, and the crown fills with enough bees to hear from the bench underneath.
trees.access: In the garden of the Bernhardskirche in Rohracker; open to visitors during the day, free, no ticket.
trees.transport: Bus 62 to the Rohracker stop, then a short walk

best_time.label: late June and early July, when the lime flowers and the crown hums with bees

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the lime shading the church garden, where the parish invites people to sit. It stands in front of the Bernhardskirche in Rohracker.

trees.name: The Hutteneiche

location.address: Vaihinger Wald, Rohrer Höhe, near the A8, Stuttgart-Vaihingen

trees.story:
On 7 May 1515 Duke Ulrich of Württemberg took his stable master out hunting in this forest and killed him. The dead man was Hans von Hutten, and the quarrel is usually told as a matter of the duke pursuing Hutten's wife. By the tradition attached to this spot, Ulrich then hung the body from an oak, and the oak standing here carries the name.

Be careful about what that does and does not mean. No source claims the tree you walk to is the same individual that stood here in 1515; the story belongs to the place, and this tree inherited it. Two independent accounts, an encyclopedia entry and a walkers' trail note, tell it the same way, which is about as far as a five-hundred-year-old rumour can be corroborated.

Nobody has dated this oak or measured its girth, and we would rather say so than invent a number. If you know its age, tell us.

It is not on Stuttgart's list of 89 official natural monuments, so it stands here on its history rather than on any designation. The city did put up a signboard naming it in the forest in January 2013, which is how most walkers find it at all.

One honest warning about the walk. The pin marks the point our sources give, and a visitor's note puts the trunk roughly 130 metres southeast of the signpost, off the marked path. Expect to hunt for it a little.
trees.access: In the public Vaihinger Wald, a working state forest open to walkers; a signpost erected in the forest in January 2013 points visitors toward the tree from the main path.
trees.transport: S-Bahn to Stuttgart-Vaihingen or Rohr, then a walk into the forest
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the signboard the city put up in the forest in January 2013, which names it. Nobody has dated or measured the tree, and it carries no designation of its own.

trees.name: The Oberdorfplatz Mulberry
trees.story:
Stuttgart protects this mulberry for three reasons, and one of them is culture. The city's register normally gives a tree character and habitat value and leaves it there. This one was designated in June 2003 for its character, its rarity and its cultural significance, a combination that says the register is protecting the kind of tree as much as the individual trunk.

It stands on the Oberdorfplatz, the square of the old village centre of Möhringen, which is now a Stuttgart district with trams running through it. Nobody has written down who put the tree there or why, and mulberries have been planted in Europe for two reasons, their fruit and their leaves, which feed silkworms. What is on record is that this one has watched the village around it stop being a village.

Two things we cannot tell you. Nobody has published an age or a girth for it, so we are not going to invent one. And no source says whether it is a black mulberry or a white one, which is a thing you could settle standing in front of it: white mulberry leaves are glossy, black mulberry leaves are rough as sandpaper. Tell us which you find.

The last photograph we can point to was taken in March 2017, and it names the tree by its exact register number.
trees.access: On Oberdorfplatz, a public square in the old village centre of Möhringen; free, open at all times.
trees.transport: Stadtbahn to Möhringen Rathaus, short walk

best_time.label: July and August, when the fruit ripens and drops onto the square

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the mulberry standing on Oberdorfplatz, in the old village centre of Möhringen. Look closely at the leaves, glossy if white mulberry, rough as sandpaper if black.

trees.name: The Bald Cypresses of the Kurpark
trees.story:
Three swamp trees from the American south, standing in a German spa park, protected by law for being unusual. Bald cypresses belong in the floodplains of the Mississippi and the Carolinas; Stuttgart designated this group a natural monument in June 2003 for its character and its rarity, which is the register admitting outright that these do not grow here by themselves.

They are also the conifer that breaks the rule about conifers. A bald cypress drops its needles every winter, and before it does, the whole crown turns a rust orange that nothing else in a German park does. In wet ground the roots send up woody knees around the trunk, so look down as well as up.

The Kurpark is Bad Cannstatt's spa park, and its tree stock dates largely from the nineteenth century. That stock is being renewed a few trees at a time, which is the ordinary fate of a maintained park.

Here is what we cannot confirm. The most recent evidence we have that these three are standing is a photograph from May 2017, tagged with their exact register number, and nothing since names them. They are almost certainly fine, and we would rather tell you that than pretend to a fresher check. If you walk past them, tell us what you find. No age or girth has ever been published for them.
trees.access: In the Kurpark in Bad Cannstatt, a free public park; open at all times, no ticket.
trees.transport: Stadtbahn to Bad Cannstatt, short walk through the Kurpark

best_time.label: November, when the needles turn rust orange and then fall

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by their needles, turning rust orange before dropping in autumn, and by woody knees rising from wet ground around the trunks. They stand in the Kurpark in Bad Cannstatt.

trees.name: The Ash at Schloss Solitude

location.address: In front of Schloss Solitude, Solitude, Stuttgart-West

trees.story:
A German tree register measured this ash in May 2026 and got 6.72 metres around the trunk, taken low at 60 centimetres. European ash does not usually reach that. The same visit recorded it 23 metres tall and, in the register's own word, vital: a thick old tree in good condition rather than a monument being propped up.

The register puts its age at 250 years. That is the register's own estimate and nobody has counted rings, so we carry it as a band, somewhere between 200 and 300 years; the tree is the same either way. It stands on the lawn in front of Schloss Solitude, the baroque hunting lodge on the ridge west of the city, whose grounds are now free and open at any hour. Only the rooms inside need a ticket.

Stuttgart protects it, but not alone. The city's ordinance designates one monument here, a group: this ash plus two sycamore maples, listed together in June 2003 for their character and as habitat. No source has measured the two maples, so the ash is the documented one and the other two are its company.

Its trunk forks low into a wide, many-branched crown, which is worth seeing bare. Come in January or February and the whole frame is legible from the grass.
trees.access: In the open green grounds in front of Schloss Solitude; free and open at all times. Only the palace interior itself requires a ticket.
trees.transport: Bus 92 to the Solitude stop, short walk

best_time.label: January and February, when the leaves are down and the low fork and full crown of branches show

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its trunk, forking low into a wide, many-branched crown, standing with two sycamore maples as its company. It stands on the lawn in front of Schloss Solitude.

official_register.name: Naturdenkmal Einzelgebilde (LUBW Schutzgebietssteckbrief), listed as Baumgruppe vor Schloss Solitude, no. 81110000506

trees.name: The Hohenheim Love Plane

location.address: Exotischer Garten, Hohenheimer Gärten, Universität Hohenheim, Garbenstraße, 70599 Stuttgart-Hohenheim

trees.access: In the free, publicly open Exotic Garden of the Hohenheimer Gärten (University of Hohenheim); open year-round, all day, no ticket. Parking on site.
trees.transport: Stadtbahn U3 to Plieningen (terminus), about 300m walk
trees.story:
Duke Carl Eugen of Wuerttemberg planted this plane in 1779, tradition says as a gesture toward the woman who would become his wife. About four metres up, the trunk splits cleanly into two, and Hohenheim has read that fork as a love story ever since: two lovers, united at the root, each still their own person in the canopy.

Whatever the duke intended, the tree has done well by it. At 34 metres it ranks among the tallest planes in Germany, with a trunk 7.70 metres round measured in December 2022, and in May 2023 the German Dendrological Society named it one of the country's Nationalerbe-Baeume, National Heritage Trees, a list of roughly a hundred. It grows in the Exotic Garden of the university's Hohenheimer Gaerten, open and free every day of the year.

Age has not made it decorative. The cavities in that quarter-millennium of wood shelter owls, dormice and bats, and the tree is one of the known German homes of the hermit beetle, a protected saproxylic species that depends on exactly this kind of old, hollowing timber. Arborists inspect it twice a year and carry out whatever care keeps a tree this size and this old standing safely over a public garden.

The Hohenheim Liebesplatane, the locals call it. Love plane.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its trunk, splitting cleanly into two about four metres up. It stands in the Exotic Garden of the Hohenheimer Gärten, at the University of Hohenheim.

trees.name: The Schillereiche

location.address: Schillerhoehe lookout, Wernhaldenstrasse above Neue Weinsteige, Stuttgart

trees.story:
This oak was planted for a play. In 1865 the Verschönerungsverein, Stuttgart's beautification society, laid out a lookout on the Schillerhöhe and put this tree on it. By the club's own account it marks the first reading of Schiller's Die Räuber; a newspaper agrees on the year but is vaguer about where that reading happened, so treat the link to the play as the club's story.

The planting is what makes it datable, which is rarer than it sounds. Counted from 1865 rather than guessed from a trunk, it is about 160 years old. Nobody has published its girth or height.

It has outlasted most of what was built around it. A Kurhaus and restaurant named after the oak once stood beside it and is gone. In 2005, for the 200th anniversary of Schiller's death, the lookout was renovated together with the city's parks, cemeteries and forestry office. The club still owns the ground and keeps it open as a public viewpoint, and Stuttgart has protected the oak as a natural monument since 2003.

The view is the other reason to climb up. From 408 metres the lookout takes in the city from south-west to north-east, with benches beside the trunk and a footpath along Wernhaldenstraße. A photograph from May 2024 shows the crown full and in leaf.

Pair it with the Wernhalde sequoias, about 250 metres east on the same slope.
trees.access: Free, open lookout with benches and a footpath beside Wernhaldenstrasse; the ground belongs to the Verschoenerungsverein Stuttgart, which keeps it as a public viewpoint. No ticket.
trees.transport: Stadtbahn U5/U6 to Weinsteige, then roughly 10 to 15 minutes' walk along Wernhaldenstrasse (walk time estimated, not sourced)
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the oak on the Schillerhöhe lookout, with benches beside it and the city laid out below from 408 metres. It stands by the footpath along Wernhaldenstraße.

official_register.name: Naturdenkmal Einzelgebilde 81110000403 (LUBW Schutzgebietssteckbrief, Stadt Stuttgart), no. 81110000403

trees.name: The Wernhalde Giant Sequoias

location.address: Steinkopfstrasse 6 and 8, beside the Wernhaldenpark, Stuttgart

trees.story:
Two giant sequoias stand about ten metres apart between the houses of Steinkopfstraße, and Stuttgart protects each one under its own number. The trees at number 6 and number 8 were made natural monuments in June 2003; we list them as one stop, because you will see them together.

Sequoias are something of a Stuttgart habit. A local walking writer traces many of the ones in the city and across Württemberg to King Wilhelm I, who bought a pound of seed in 1864, and describes the sequoias in the Wernhaldenpark next door as reaching sizes unbelievable for Württemberg. Whether these two grew from that pound of seed, nobody has recorded. Their planting date is not documented, and we are not going to borrow the king's year for them. If you know when they went in, tell us.

The official register is the only source that names these two individually, and it gives no girth or height. A photograph from April 2018 shows a tall, healthy conifer behind a roadside rail, with houses beside it.

Be clear about access. They stand between houses on ground no source describes, so these are trees to look at from the street and footpath, not to walk up to, and the pin is the register's approximate point. For sequoias you can stand under, the public Wernhaldenpark next door has many more on its steep paths, along with a young planting from 1990 not to be mistaken for the old ones.
trees.access: View-only from the public street and footpath beside Steinkopfstrasse (visible over a fence in the Commons photo); the tree itself stands between houses and its plot status is not stated by any source. The Wernhaldenpark next door is public, with five entrances, steep paths and many more sequoias.
trees.transport: Stadtbahn U5/U6 to Weinsteige, then about 10 minutes down Roemerstrasse into the park (per stuttgartwege blog route; time estimated)
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the two giant sequoias about ten metres apart between the houses at Steinkopfstraße 6 and 8. You see them from the street over a fence, beside the Wernhaldenpark.

official_register.name: Naturdenkmal Einzelgebilde 81110000027 (LUBW Schutzgebietssteckbrief, Stadt Stuttgart), no. 81110000027

trees.name: The Jahneiche

location.address: Marconistrasse at the end of Lange Allee, Zuffenhausen, Stuttgart

trees.story:
By 1711 this oak was already called a stately old tree, and a duke chose it as the spot for his hunting lodge. That is the account in the German Wikipedia: Duke Eberhard Ludwig of Württemberg had a hunting pavilion built beside it for his Schlotwiese hunting ground. We have not seen the 1711 record behind the claim, so we carry it as Wikipedia's and put the tree's age no closer than over 300 years. Nobody has measured the trunk to test that. If the 1711 mention holds, it is the oldest tree on this page.

The name is far younger than the tree. In 1929 the Turnverein Zuffenhausen, the district's gymnastics club, marked its 40th anniversary by naming the oak after Friedrich Ludwig Jahn, the Turnvater of German gymnastics. A tree that stood in a duke's hunting ground now carries a gymnastics club's birthday present.

It has not had an untroubled old age. Some years ago, a local newspaper reported, a gust of wind broke off a heavy branch and the area around it was cordoned off. The report is no longer online. Stuttgart has protected the oak as a natural monument since 2003, and a photograph from April 2020 names it.

It stands where Lange Allee ends at Marconistraße. The pin is the register's approximate point, and no source describes whether the trunk sits on a verge or a green strip. If you go, tell us what you find, and its girth if you can measure it.
trees.access: Standing at the junction of Lange Allee and Marconistrasse, a public street junction; no ticket. Exact surroundings (verge or green strip) not confirmed.
trees.transport: Zuffenhausen, Stuttgart; nearest stop not checked (S-Bahn Zuffenhausen is in the district, walk time unknown)
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the old oak at the junction where Lange Allee ends at Marconistraße in Zuffenhausen. Another protected oak stands about 70 metres north-east; this is the one on the junction.

official_register.name: Naturdenkmal Einzelgebilde 81110000903 (LUBW Schutzgebietssteckbrief, Stadt Stuttgart), no. 81110000903
